title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Marcus Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also includes a small set of canonical ADRs that capture recent, high-impact decisions. The goal is to provide a single reference for architects and engineers to make consistent, auditable technical choices that support our production SLOs and operational model.

Audience and scope
- Audience: Engineers, tech leads, architects, and reviewers working on runtime, serving, infra, and SDKs.
- Scope: All services that implement customer-facing APIs or contribute to inference serving, the control plane, and platform observability. Private deployment documentation supplements these standards where customer constraints differ.

Principles (applies across sections)
- Consistency: APIs and service patterns must be predictable across teams.
- Observable by design: All services must emit metrics, traces, and structured logs for critical paths.
- Fail-safe and graceful degradation: Design fallbacks for overloaded or failed dependencies.
- Cost-consciousness: Prefer patterns that reduce per-token cost (caching, batching) without violating latency SLOs.
- Security first: Least privilege, encrypted-in-transit and at-rest for customer data; follow security-and-compliance controls.

1) API standards
Purpose: Ensure stable, versioned, and easy-to-consume APIs for hosted, dedicated, and private customers.

1.1 Contract and versioning
- Semantic versioning for public contract changes: PATCH = non-breaking fixes; MINOR = additive, backward-compatible features; MAJOR = breaking changes or incompatible defaults.
- All public API surfaces must publish a contract (OpenAPI v3) and example client snippets.
- Backwards compatibility window: maintain previous MINOR for at least 90 days before sunsetting.

1.2 REST and idempotency
- Primary external APIs are JSON-over-HTTP with well-defined status codes.
- Use idempotency keys for start-of-work operations (idempotency-key header).
- Streaming endpoints use text/event-stream or gRPC bidi streams with chunk framing and explicit end markers.

1.3 Request and response shape
- Top-level response envelope: {"request_id", "status", "data", "warnings"} for external endpoints. Include deterministic field names.
- Pagination: cursor-based (opaque cursor), limit parameter with max enforced at 1000 unless approved.
- Error schema: consistent error object with code, description, retriable (boolean), and troubleshooting_url.

1.4 Rate limiting and quotas
- Implement per-customer and per-route rate limits. Include a Retry-After header for 429 responses.
- Expose quota usage endpoints for customers and SDKs.

1.5 Examples and SDK guidance
- Provide example OpenAPI snippets and a canonical cURL/HTTP example in docs.
- SDKs must map 1:1 to public contracts where feasible and document deviations.

API example (canonical response envelope)
{"request_id": "r_12345", "status": "ok", "data": {"output": "..."}, "warnings": []}

2) Coding standards
Purpose: Improve readability, testability, and maintainability across Redwood services.

2.1 Language and style
- Service backends: primarily Go (server runtime and infra) and Python (ML tooling and small orchestration). New services should default to Go for high-throughput paths.
- Style guides: follow effective Go (gofmt, go vet), Black + isort for Python, and ESLint/Prettier for TypeScript.

2.2 Testing
- Unit tests: aim for feature-complete unit tests with table-driven patterns in Go; coverage target is >= 60% for new services.
- Integration tests: every service must include integration tests that run against a test harness or local emulation for key external dependencies.
- CI gating: PRs must pass lint, unit tests, and a lightweight integration suite before merge.

2.3 Dependency control and security
- Pin third-party dependencies and run automated dependency scanning (Snyk/OSS). Require security review for any dependency with CPE/known CVE.
- Minimum supported language/runtime versions documented in repo README.

2.4 Code review and ownership
- Default reviewer is the service owner + one peer reviewer. Major changes require an architecture review. Use ADRs for long-lived design changes.

3) Infrastructure standards
Purpose: Ensure secure, repeatable, and observable infrastructure deployments for hosted and private offerings.

3.1 IaC and environments
- All infrastructure must be declared in Terraform modules stored in the terraform-and-iac directory. Use modules for common patterns (iam, networking, autoscaling).
- Environment parity: dev -> staging -> prod parity must be maintained for critical configs (scaling rules, instance types).

3.2 Networking and security
- VPC design: apply standardized subnetting and egress controls; use shared services for central logging and KMS.
- Private deployments: document customer-managed networking and required firewall rules in eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures.

3.3 Capacity and autoscaling
- Use target tracking autoscaling tied to custom metrics where helpful (e.g., queued-request-depth or GPU-utilization).
- Each service must have an SLO-driven capacity plan (see eng-sre/capacity-planning).

3.4 Secrets and key management
- Secrets in KMS or cloud-managed secret store; no plaintext secrets in repo. For private/offline deployments, document KMS/HSM integration steps.

Infra config table (example)
| Component | Minimum prod | Recommended | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Control-plane API (replicas) | 3 | 3+ across AZs | Regional HA required |
| GPU inference pool (p3p4 or equivalent) | 2 nodes per shard | autoscale to 10 | Use GPU-optimized AMIs |
| Logging retention | 30 days | 90 days (paying customers) | Longer for compliance customers |

4) Model-serving standards
Purpose: Provide consistent behavior for latency, caching, batching, and model varianting across the serving runtime.

4.1 Model artifact requirements
- Model metadata: every model must publish a manifest (JSON) with fields: model_id, version, architecture, tokenizer, max_seq_len, quantization_profile, compatible_kernels.
- Packaging: container images for runtime, OCI-compatible blobs for model binaries, and an index in the model catalog.

4.2 Execution and kernel selection
- Runtime must select kernels based on sequence-length percentiles and model architecture. Prefer vectorized attention kernels where supported.
- Quantization: maintain profiles for int8/4 that are validated by the quantization-profiles test suite.

4.3 Caching and batching
- Automatic prefix/KV caching with explicit cache-control metadata in manifest.
- Batching: continuous batching layer must respect per-request latency SLOs. Default batch time window is 10ms for 99th-percentile-sensitive routes; tunable per-route.

4.4 Model rollout and fallbacks
- Use canary + gradual rollout with traffic percentage controls. Always define fallback model variants and an automatic policy to fallback on increased error rate or latency regressions.
- Observe model quality: tie prompt-level evals to deployment and alert on regressions.

Model manifest example (text)
{
  "model_id": "redwood-bert-l2",
  "version": "2026-02-01",
  "architecture": "transformer",
  "tokenizer": "byte-bpe",
  "max_seq_len": "2048",
  "quantization_profile": "int8-standard",
  "compatible_kernels": ["vec-attn-v1", "kv-cache-opt"]
}

5) Observability standards
Purpose: Provide a unified signals surface (metrics, traces, logs) to troubleshoot, measure, and automate.

5.1 Metrics (prometheus style)
- Instrumentation: counters, gauges, histograms must follow metric naming conventions (service_component_metric).
- Cardinality: labels limited to low-cardinality keys (customer_id only in aggregated metrics, use hashing/rollups for privacy).
- Required metrics for any service: requests_total, requests_failed_total, request_latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), cpu_utilization, memory_usage_bytes. For inference services add tokens_generated_total and batch_size_histogram.

5.2 Tracing
- Distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry. All RPCs must propagate trace context and include request_id and model_id as trace attributes.

5.3 Logging
- Structured JSON logs at INFO and above for important state transitions; DEBUG logs gated behind runtime flags. Log format must include timestamp, request_id, level, component, message, and context fields.

5.4 Dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: per-service overview (error rate, latency p50/p95/p99, throughput), per-model health.
- Alerting: use symptom-based alerts (e.g., increased 5m error rate > 0.5% over baseline, p99 latency > SLO). Include runbook links.

6) Performance standards and SLOs
Purpose: Define company-wide SLOs for customer-facing inference and internal control-plane services.

6.1 Default SLO targets
- Inference (hosted API): 99th percentile tail latency for streaming endpoints <= 300ms for short-completions (<=64 tokens); for long-completions (>=512 tokens) percentile targets measured in token-generation throughput (tokens/sec) per GPU shard. Availability (4xx/5xx) >= 99.95%.
- Control plane APIs: 99th percentile latency <= 250ms for concisely-scoped calls; availability >= 99.9%.

6.2 Performance budgeting and reviews
- Every major feature needs a performance budget documented in PRD and a perf-runbook in benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Perf regressions: failing a benchmark triggers a performance triage (see regression-triage).

7) ADRs (Decision records)
This section captures a small set of canonical decisions. Each ADR follows: title, status, context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered, owners, and date.

ADR-2025-09: Runtime language choice for hot path
- Status: accepted
- Context: need a language/runtime for low-latency GPU-serving control-plane hooks and request routing.
- Decision: choose Go for hot path services (dispatcher, routing, control-plane endpoints) and Python for model offline tooling and evals.
- Consequences: improved GC characteristics and binary deployment for services that must manage many goroutines; need for interop patterns between Go and Python services (gRPC).
- Alternatives: Rust (rejected due to team capacity and ecosystem maturity at the time), Java (heavier memory footprint).
- Owner: Marcus Chen
- Date: 2025-09-15

ADR-2026-01: Default quantization profile strategy
- Status: accepted
- Context: reduce inference unit costs while preserving quality for customer workloads.
- Decision: adopt int8-standard as default quantization profile for throughput-optimized internal model variants; maintain fp16 for high-quality variants.
- Consequences: requires expanded QA and per-model validation in quantization-profiles test suite; update model manifest to include profile and measured regression thresholds.
- Alternatives: use mixed-precision on per-model basis (rejected as operationally complex).
- Owner: Aisha Patel
- Date: 2026-01-24

Process for new ADRs
1. Open ADR PR in architecture-and-standards with a short title and status=proposed.
2. Include context, alternatives, decision, consequences, and roll-back plan.
3. Assign at least two reviewers from affected teams.
4. ADR is accepted after reviewers sign-off and noted in last_updated.

Related pages
- architecture-standards-unified-guidelines-adrs-2026-03-01 (canonical guidelines)
- eng-sre/capacity-planning (capacity planning templates)
- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (runtime architecture deep-dive)

Ownership and maintenance
- Primary owner: Architecture and Standards guild (eng-platform + eng-serving-runtime).
- Review cadence: annual review or sooner when major platform changes occur.
- How to propose changes: submit a PR to this document and create an ADR for significant design changes.

Appendix: Quickcheck list for PR reviewers
- API: Is the public contract backward compatible? Is there an OpenAPI spec?
- Observability: Are required metrics/traces/logs present?
- Performance: Is there a perf budget and a microbenchmark?
- Security: Any customer data in logs or metrics? Are secrets handled correctly?

Appendix: Useful snippets
- cURL example (inference):
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":"Translate to French: Hello world","max_tokens":32}'

- Prometheus metric naming example: redwood_inference_model_request_latency_seconds_bucket{service="inference",model_id="redwood-bert-l2"} 12345

End of document.
